Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'three phrases' (三句: 三, 'three,' plus 句, 'phrase, clause, or line'). In the records this is a structural label for a master's or house's words arranged as a triad. Eye of Humans and Gods (人天眼目) catalogues Linji's three phrases (臨濟三句), Yunmen's three phrases (雲門三句), and Fenyang's three phrases (汾陽三句) in parallel sections. Fenyang's set is 'the phrase on which one exerts strength, the phrase for turning the body, and the intimate phrase' (著力句 / 轉身句 / 親切句), demonstrating that the same three-phrase form can contain a different set. A triad can be raised outside its originating house: Yunmen raises Linji's three-phrase saying and questions a stupa keeper about it (舉臨濟三句語問塔主). The variants 'three-phrase saying' (三句語, 38 occurrences) and 'outside the three phrases' (三句外, 102) show the label circulating as a unit. The two most frequently cited, and differently constituted, triads have their own senses below.
Senses.Note: A corpus-wide structural sense. The phrase names the triadic form, not one invariant set: Linji, Yunmen, and Fenyang fill it differently.

Occurrences.Kwic: 汾陽上堂僧出問。如何是學人著力句。汾云。嘉州打大像。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Eye of Humans and Gods (人天眼目), section on Fenyang's three phrases (汾陽三句). Fenyang Shanzhao's set consists of the phrase on which one exerts strength, the phrase for turning the body, and the intimate phrase (著力句 / 轉身句 / 親切句), one house-specific filling of the form.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師舉臨濟三句語問塔主。祇如塔中和尚得第幾句。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Compendium of the Five Lamps (五燈會元), Yunmen section. Yunmen raises Linji's three-phrase saying (臨濟三句語) and asks a stupa keeper which phrase the monk in the stupa attained. This shows a triad circulating across houses.

Senses.Explanation: The set called Yunmen's three phrases consists of 'enclosing heaven and earth' (函蓋乾坤句), 'cutting off the myriad streams' (截斷眾流句), and 'following the waves and pursuing the swells' (隨波逐浪句). The corpus explicitly distinguishes Yunmen's original words from the later three-part formulation. Yunmen addresses the assembly with 'enclosing heaven and earth; the eye weighs to the smallest measure; not touching the myriad conditions' (函蓋乾坤，目機銖兩，不涉萬緣), or with the variant 'not touching spring conditions' (不涉春緣). When no one answers, he supplies 'one arrowhead breaks three barriers' (一鏃破三關). Eye of Humans and Gods then says that his heir Deshan Yuanming split Yunmen's words into three phrases (後來德山圓明密禪師，遂離其語為三句) and names the set. Thereafter monks ask masters about each member in turn. This sense therefore records the triad conventionally named for Yunmen while retaining the corpus's statement that Deshan Yuanming made the three-part formulation.
Senses.Note: A genuinely distinct named triad, so the sense remains keyed to Yunmen. The text nevertheless says that Deshan Yuanming codified it from Yunmen's words (遂離其語為三句); it was not an utterance in which Yunmen himself listed the three later names. The constituent phrases also circulate independently: 'enclosing heaven and earth' (函蓋乾坤), 189 occurrences; 'cutting off the myriad streams' (截斷眾流), 370; 'following the waves and pursuing the swells' (隨波逐浪), 360.

Occurrences.Kwic: 後來德山圓明密禪師。遂離其語為三句。曰函蓋乾坤句。截斷眾流句。隨波逐浪句。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Eye of Humans and Gods (人天眼目), section on the three phrases (三句). The compiler states that Deshan Yuanming split Yunmen's words into three phrases (遂離其語為三句) and then names all three members. This is the corpus's account of the formulation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 示眾云天中函蓋乾坤目機銖兩。不涉春緣。作麼生承當。代云。一鏃破三關。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Extensive Record of Chan Master Yunmen Kuangzhen (雲門匡真禪師廣錄), demonstrations and substitute words (垂示代語). Yunmen's own record preserves his original lines and self-answer, 'one arrowhead breaks three barriers' (一鏃破三關), from which the later triad was drawn.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。如何是函蓋乾坤句。師曰。天上有星皆拱北。曰。如何是截斷眾流句。師曰。大地坦
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Compendium of the Five Lamps (五燈會元), entry for Chan Master Xichan Qin in Xinzhou (信州西禪欽禪師). A monk asks about each phrase in turn, showing the completed triad circulating as a standard series of questions.

Senses.Explanation: Linji's first, second, and third phrases (第一句 / 第二句 / 第三句), distinguished by rank. Linji says: attain it in the first phrase and you are a teacher of Buddhas and patriarchs; attain it in the second and you are a teacher of humans and gods; attain it in the third and you cannot even save yourself (若第一句中得，與祖佛為師；若第二句中得，與人天為師；若第三句中得，自救不了). Each phrase also receives a recorded answer. Asked 'What is the first phrase?' (如何是第一句), Linji replies that the seal of the three essentials opens with the vermilion mark narrow, and before deliberation is allowed host and guest are divided (三要印開朱點側，未容擬議主賓分). Eye of Humans and Gods collects the exchange, restates the ranking, and adds later comments. This is a different triad from the one named for Yunmen.
Senses.Note: A genuinely distinct Linji set. The compound 'Linji's three-phrase saying' (臨濟三句語) is raised in other houses. Linji's own record uses the ordinal names first, second, and third phrase; Eye of Humans and Gods titles the section 'three phrases' (三句).

Occurrences.Kwic: 若第一句中得，與祖佛為師；若第二句中得，與人天為師；若第三句中得，自救不了。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Linji Huizhao of Zhenzhou (鎮州臨濟慧照禪師語錄), in a hall address (上堂). Linji gives the graded ranking of the first, second, and third phrases. This is his own recorded speech.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：「如何是第一句？」師云：「三要印開朱點側，未容擬議主賓分。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Linji (臨濟錄), in a hall address (上堂). Asked 'What is the first phrase?' (如何是第一句), Linji gives its recorded answer; the second and third follow immediately.

Occurrences.Kwic: 第一句薦得。堪與佛祖為師。第二句薦得。堪與人天為師。第三句薦得。自救不了。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Eye of Humans and Gods (人天眼目), section on Linji's three phrases (臨濟三句). The compiler restates Linji's ranking and then records comments by later masters.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, three inches. In Chan speech the bare measure repeatedly abbreviates 'the three-inch tongue': one master says, 'I have one mouth, containing a three-inch tongue; the teeth are all complete, and there is no right or wrong it does not speak' (I have one mouth, containing a three-inch tongue; the teeth are all complete, and there is no right or wrong it does not speak). Questions ask a master to speak 'without borrowing the three inches' (without borrowing the three inches), and appraisals call a monk's 'three inches' tight or guarded. The omitted noun is recoverable from the explicit full form and from predicates of speaking. This is the major Zen-loaded sense: an ordinary measure becomes shorthand for the speaking organ in public exchange.
Senses.Note: This sense is not split into praise and criticism of speech; those are different readings of the same tongue referent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我有一張口，內含三寸舌。牙齒總完全，是非無不說。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baoning Renyong supplies the explicit expanded noun: 'a three-inch tongue.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。不借三寸。請師道。師曰。茶堂裏貶剝去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks Lingzhao to speak 'without borrowing the three inches,' showing the bare measure as shorthand for the tongue.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老和尚三寸甚密。師曰：眾眼難謾。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk appraises the old master's 'three inches' as very guarded; the master answers, 'the eyes of the assembly are hard to deceive.'

Senses.Explanation: As an actual measure, it marks spatial distance. In the Boatman's case, Decheng says, 'the line hangs a thousand feet, its intent in the deep pool; three inches from the hook, why do you not speak?' (the line hangs a thousand feet, its intent in the deep pool; three inches from the hook, why do you not speak?). Commentarial verses preserve 'three inches from the hook' as the case's fixed wording. A measured gap is a different thing from the tongue shorthand.
Senses.Note: The fishing construction governs this sense; it is not reassigned to the tongue merely because the next action concerns speaking.

Occurrences.Kwic: 垂絲千尺。意在深潭。離鉤三寸。子何不道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Boatman Decheng's case: 'three inches from the hook' is an explicit spatial construction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 蘆葦蕭蕭江岸秋，長天獨月向西流。離鈎三寸無人道，笑倚蘭橈自點頭。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wujin Jushi's verse on the Boatman case repeats 'three inches from the hook,' anchoring its later commentarial circulation.

Senses.Explanation: With skin or face as the measured object, the phrase states thickness. One discourse says Huangbo was still 'three inches thick in the skin of his face' (the skin of his face was three inches thick). This countable dimension is neither tongue nor fishing distance, though English uses the same unit.
Senses.Note: The object being measured, face-skin, fixes this sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 未免面皮厚三寸。且道靈隱恁麼批判，意在什麼處？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A formal discourse measures face-skin as 'three inches thick.'

Senses.PreferredTarget: the last three inches of breath
Senses.Explanation: In mortality warnings, 'the three-inch breath' is the small remaining span of breath whose ending is death. Tianru says, 'when the three-inch breath is cut off, one fire burns through, and what is gathered is one pinch of cold ash' (when the three-inch breath is cut off, one fire burns through, and what is gathered is one pinch of cold ash). The explicit breath noun and the predicate 'cut off' establish a different referent from tongue, space, and thickness.
Senses.Note: The full compound 'three-inch breath' controls the elliptical English target.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三寸氣斷，一火洞然
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tianru Weize's general address names 'the three-inch breath' and describes its ending at death.

AlternateTargets: a named state of complete command
Senses.Explanation: The three graphs form an established phonetic borrowing, rendered here as 'complete command'; the Chan corpus determines its usable content through named compounds and direct definitions. The term occurs 4,852 times in 382 allowed texts. Huineng defines 'complete command of the single conduct' as 'at every place, while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, always carry one straight mind' (一行三昧者，於一切處行住坐臥，常行一直心是也). The same address rejects the claim that 'not raising thought while constantly sitting unmoving is complete command of the single conduct' (常坐不動，妄不起心，即是一行三昧), saying that this understanding is like the insentient and blocks the Way. Mazu's record says that thought after thought becoming still is called 'complete command of the ocean seal,' which 'takes in all things as a hundred thousand different streams return together to the great sea' (喚作海印三昧攝一切法如百千異流同歸大海). It also says beings remain within 'complete command of the nature of the teaching' while dressing, eating, speaking, responding, using the six sense-roots, and carrying out every action (法性三昧中著衣喫飯言談祇對六根運用一切施為). Xuansha says that buddhas are people's 'self-receiving complete command' and that walking, standing, sitting, and lying down have never not been it; when asked what that complete command is, he replies, 'What use are so many modes of complete command?' (用如許多三昧作麼). The word therefore appears as the head of explicitly named states or domains whose predicates vary by text; this entry does not collapse those names into one imported definition.
Senses.Note: Direct formula harvesting found many definitions of compounds rather than one definition of the bare headword. The article foregrounds the richest Chan self-definitions and Xuansha's corrective answer. The Chinese is historically a phonetic borrowing, but this English dictionary translates it as 'complete command' and lets each compound's recorded predicates define its local use.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一行三昧者，於一切處行住坐臥，常行一直心是也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Platform Record, section four. Huineng directly defines complete command of the single conduct through conduct in all four postures.

Occurrences.Kwic: 妄不起心，即是一行三昧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the same address Huineng quotes the claim that not raising thought while sitting unmoving is complete command of the single conduct, then explicitly rejects that understanding as like the insentient and obstructing the Way.

Occurrences.Kwic: 念念寂滅喚作海印三昧攝一切法如百千異流同歸大海
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ancient Worthies Record, Mazu's broad record. Mazu calls it complete command of the ocean seal and immediately compares its inclusion of all things to streams returning to the sea.

Occurrences.Kwic: 長在法性三昧中著衣喫飯言談祇對六根運用一切施為盡是法性
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Mazu's record says beings remain in complete command of the nature of the teaching while dressing, eating, speaking, responding, using the senses, and carrying out every action.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是自受用三昧？師云：用如許多三昧作麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuansha's Extended Record. Asked 'What is self-receiving complete command?' Xuansha replies, 'What use are so many modes of complete command?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸佛，只是諸人自受用三昧，行住坐臥未曾不是。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuansha's own address: buddhas are people's self-receiving complete command, and walking, standing, sitting, and lying down have never not been it.

Senses.Explanation: In this proper-name use, Sanmei identifies a named master rather than denoting 'complete command.' The records place 'Master Sanmei' (三昧和尚) in portrait headings, call him 'a model for people and gods' (人天模範), and record a monk receiving full ordination from him (從三昧和尚受具). These predicates belong to a person: this sense is therefore separate from compounds such as 'complete command of the single conduct' (一行三昧). The surviving witnesses also place this named master in the precept and ordination family, not in a definition of the phonetic word.
Senses.Note: Split under #0f.8 as word versus person/title. The exact form 'Master Sanmei' occurs in multiple independent allowlisted records. MasterName and SenseKey remain null because no exact canonical roster identity was established; the proper-name sense is corpus-wide lexicographic structure, not a claim of master-specific meaning.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三昧和尚珍重木叉，人天模範，光嚴住持，不離如幻，數珠百八常攜手，揚盡尸羅啟後昆。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xiaotang's record, portrait verse headed 'Master Sanmei.' It praises the named man as a model for people and gods and refers to the monastic code and precepts. No exact roster identity was assigned.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三昧和尚像久嚮嘉名，今幸得遇，果是人天軌範，大好法身常住。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhuanyu Heng's record, 'Portrait of Master Sanmei': 'Long have I admired your fine name; now happily meeting you, you are indeed a model for people and gods.' The title is a person's name.

Occurrences.Kwic: 二十一從三昧和尚受具，遂參報恩玉林和尚。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Chan Lamp of the Brocade River records that at twenty-one the subject received full ordination from Master Sanmei and then visited Master Yulin of Bao'en. Sanmei is the ordaining person.

AlternateTargets: the three mysterious gates and three essentials
Senses.Explanation: (三玄) = three "mysterious / dark" (玄 — his "mysterious gates" (玄門)); (三要) = three "essentials, pivots" (要). The source formula is in Linji (臨濟義玄)'s record: "one phrase of speech must be furnished with three mysterious gates; each mysterious gate must be furnished with three essentials; there is (權) [the provisional / expedient] and there is (用) [function]" (一句語須具三玄門，一玄門須具三要，有權、有用). In his three-phrase teaching the (三要) also surfaces: (如何是第一句)？」(師云)：「"the seal of the three essentials lifts, the vermilion dot beside it; before you can deliberate, host and guest are divided" (三要印開朱點側，未容擬議主賓分). In the Linji lu itself the four-character compound occurs once, in the record's prefatory matter (若夫三玄三要奪境奪人，金章玉句如風檣陣馬), not in Linji's recorded speech. The compound is in Fenyang (汾陽善昭)'s own record — (一句中有三玄三要)。(賓主歷然) — and in his verse "the three mysteries and three essentials are hard to parse; get the meaning, forget the words, and the Way is easy to reach" (三玄三要事難分。得意忘言道易親). The handbook (人天眼目) gives an enumeration — (三玄者)。(玄中玄)。(體中玄)。(句中玄)。(三要者)。(一玄中具三要)。(自是一喝中)。(體攝三玄三要也) — naming the three (玄) but stating of the (要) only that each (玄) holds three, and that a single shout "embraces the three mysteries and three essentials" (體攝三玄三要). Across the record (455× in 157 allowlist files) the compound runs in a fixed device-list, (三玄三要四料揀)，(一喝分賓主)，(照用一時行) (9× in 7 files, e.g. J36nB356), and such lists assign it to the Linji house: (要知臨濟家蜂子麼)？(四料揀)、(四賓主)、(三玄三要者是) (J29nB233). It is also posed as a test question, (如何是三玄三要) (7 allowlist files), drawing recorded answers — (何必重拈舊葛藤) (J39nB452), (次第問來) (J39nB471), a blow and (龍頭蛇尾得人憎) (J38nB428) — typically followed by the item-by-item sequence (如何是第一玄)／(第二玄)／(第三玄), which masters answer line by line (第一玄: 178× in 110 files).
Senses.Note: Render the graphs literally as mysteries and essentials. Linji's recorded speech gives the layering formula—'one phrase,' 'three gates of mystery,' and 'three essentials' (一句、三玄門、三要)—plus answers concerning the first, second, and third phrases. The fixed enumerations 'mystery within substance, mystery within the phrase, and mystery within mystery' (體中玄、句中玄、玄中玄) appear in Fenyang's record and later handbooks, not in Linji's own record, and they vary between texts. 'Provisional' (權) and 'function' (用) are translated where those graphs occur. Evidence comes from Linji's record (T47n1985), Fenyang's record (T47n1992), and the Eyes of Humans and Gods handbook (人天眼目, T48n2006).

Occurrences.Kwic: 一句語須具三玄門，一玄門須具三要，有權、有用。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (鎮州臨濟慧照禪師語錄) (the Linji lu); (師) = (臨濟義玄). The source formula from which the compound (三玄三要) derives — a single teaching-phrase must be layered into three mysterious gates, each into three essentials, holding both (權) and (用).

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是第一句？」師云：「三要印開朱點側，未容擬議主賓分。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji lu; (師) = (臨濟義玄), answering (如何是第一句). Where (三要) first appears inside his first/second/third-phrase teaching — the seal of the three essentials, host and guest divided before thought.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一句中有三玄三要。賓主歷然。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (汾陽無德禪師語錄); (師) = (汾陽善昭). The compound in Fenyang's own prose — within one phrase there are three mysteries and three essentials, host and guest plainly distinct.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三玄三要事難分。得意忘言道易親。一句分明該萬象。重陽九日菊花新。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (汾陽無德禪師語錄); Fenyang's verse on (三玄三要) (this record reads 一句分明該萬象; 人天眼目's copy reads 明明).

Occurrences.Kwic: 三玄者。玄中玄。體中玄。句中玄。三要者。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (人天眼目) (a Chan handbook, 臨濟宗 section) — editorial exposition laying out the standard enumeration of the three (玄); not a single master's saying, hence null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 自是一喝中。體攝三玄三要也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (人天眼目) exposition — the whole schema collapses into one shout, which "embraces the three mysteries and three essentials." Corpus-wide editorial voice, null.

AlternateTargets: the three realms are only mind
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “the three realms are mind-only.” The compound often stands beside “the myriad things are consciousness-only,” and one prose passage calls the pair “the root principle that is realized” and “the central statement that can explain.” Chan encounter records also put the words into questions. Xuansha asks Guichen how he understands them; Guichen points to a chair, and both men call the chair wood. In another case, a teacher points to a stone and asks a lecturer who habitually says the formula whether the stone is inside or outside mind. The headword occurs 248 times across 88 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: One proposition throughout. Expository assertion and interview testing are distinct deployments, not distinct things.

Occurrences.Kwic: 經云。三界唯心。萬法唯識。此是所證本理。能詮正宗
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An expository record pairs the formula with the myriad things being consciousness-only and labels it the stated principle.

Occurrences.Kwic: 故三界唯心。森羅萬象。一法之所印。凡所見色。皆是見心
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp-record address states the formula and continues that the manifold appearances are stamped by one thing and seen form is seeing mind.

Occurrences.Kwic: 沙問。三界唯心。汝作麼生會。師指倚子曰。和尚喚這箇作甚麼
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuansha asks Guichen how he understands the formula; Guichen points to a chair and asks what Xuansha calls it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我喚這箇作竹木。汝喚作甚麼。師曰。桂琛亦喚作竹木
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The chair exchange continues with Xuansha and Guichen both calling the object bamboo and wood.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上座尋常說三界唯心，萬法唯識。乃指庭下片石曰：且道此石在心內，在心外
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher points to a courtyard stone and asks a lecturer who habitually states the paired formula whether the stone is inside or outside mind.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Xuansha's three kinds of impaired person
AlternateTargets: the blind, deaf, and mute people
Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘three kinds of impaired person.’ In Xuansha Shibei's recorded challenge they are a blind person who cannot see a raised mallet or whisk, a deaf person who cannot hear speech, and a mute person who cannot answer. Xuansha asks how the elders who claim to receive people and benefit living beings would receive them, and says that failure to receive them leaves the buddha-teaching without efficacy. A monk asks permission to discuss the three, says farewell, and is twice rejected with ‘not so’; Luohan Guichen then asks how Xuansha would receive him although Guichen has eyes, ears, and a mouth, and Xuansha withdraws to his quarters. Yunmen's later handling begins by ordering the questioner to bow. Elsewhere the phrase itself is asked as a public-interview question and receives ‘you have just asked it.’ Thus the corpus bends a medical enumeration into Xuansha's named teaching-seat challenge about an encounter in which seeing, hearing, and answering are unavailable; this entry reports the recorded moves without supplying their unstated intent.
Senses.Note: The named referent is Xuansha's fixed blind/deaf/mute triad, so the master key records a genuinely master-specific thing. Later records, verses, and comments preserve and answer that same case rather than introducing a second sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祇如三種病人。汝作麼生接。患盲者。拈槌竪拂他又不見。患聾者。語言三昧他又不聞。患瘂者。教伊說又說不得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuansha enumerates the blind, deaf, and mute persons and asks how they are received.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三種病人還許學人商量否。師曰。許。汝作麼生商量。其僧珍重出。師曰。不是。不是。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks to discuss the triad; Xuansha rejects his departure twice.

Occurrences.Kwic: 羅漢曰。桂琛現有眼耳口。和尚作麼生接。師曰。慚愧。便歸方丈。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Luohan Guichen turns the question onto Xuansha; the record gives Xuansha's reply and withdrawal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是三種病人。師曰。恰問著。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The phrase becomes a direct public-interview question; the answer is ‘you have just asked it.’

Senses.Explanation: Literally 'three checkpoints' or 'three barriers.' As a corpus-wide expression it can count a threefold set without identifying one universal list. Wansong explicitly says that the label includes sets associated with Baizhang, Dayang, Puan, Linji, Xuansha, and the Old Pagoda master, and is not confined to Doushuai and Huanglong. In the separate formula 'one arrow pierces three checkpoints' (一鏃破三關), Qinshan is questioned about piercing three barriers and Yunmen supplies the same line as an answer after his assembly gives no answer. These are generic countable barriers; the two recurrent named taxonomies are separated below because their three questions refer to different things.
Senses.Note: The undifferentiated headword occurs 578 times in 210 allowlisted texts. The formula 'one arrow pierces three checkpoints' (一鏃破三關) occurs 117 times in 69. Do not silently substitute either named list for a generic occurrence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所謂三關者，百丈、大陽、普安道皆有三句，臨濟、玄沙、古塔主皆有三玄等，非止兜率悅、老黃龍獨有三關也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wansong's prose explicitly broadens the label beyond the Doushuai and Huanglong sets.

Occurrences.Kwic: 巨良禪客參，禮拜了，便問：一鏃破三關時如何？師曰：放出關中主看。良曰：恁麼則知過必改。師曰：更待何時？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Juliang asks Qinshan about the formula 'when one arrow pierces three checkpoints.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：函葢乾坤，目機銖兩。不涉世緣，作麼生承當？眾無對。自代曰：一鏃破三關。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunmen supplies 'one arrow pierces three checkpoints' as his own answer after the assembly gives no answer.

Senses.Explanation: Huanglong Huinan's named three checkpoints are a fixed set of three questions: 'How is my hand like a buddha's hand?' (我手何似佛手), 'How is my foot like a donkey's foot?' (我脚何似驢脚), and 'Where is your birth-circumstance?' (上座生緣在何處). His governing section says that the Chan community called these 'Huanglong's three checkpoints' (黃龍三關). A later hall address quotes the three questions and appraises 'Huanglong's three checkpoints' as resembling Lord Shang's institution of laws. The name therefore refers to Huanglong's particular three-question set, not to Doushuai's different list.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase 'Huanglong's three checkpoints' (黃龍三關) occurs 139 times in 87 allowlisted texts. The master key is warranted because this recurrent named taxonomy has a fixed Huanglong-specific referent, not merely because Huanglong supplied an early witness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 室中舉手問僧：我手何似佛手？垂足曰：我脚何似驢脚？人人盡有生緣，上座生緣在何處？學者莫有契其旨，叢林目之為黃龍三關。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huanglong's governing section states all three questions and reports the community's fixed name for them.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂，舉黃龍南室中垂語曰：我手何似佛手？我脚何似驢脚？人人有箇生緣，那箇是上座生緣？師曰：黃龍三關，如商君立法。法雖立，而先王之道廢矣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later hall address quotes Huanglong's complete three-question set, names it 'Huanglong's three checkpoints,' and compares it to Lord Shang instituting laws.

Senses.Explanation: Doushuai Congyue's three checkpoint sayings are a different fixed set. The first asks where one's nature is now when one parts the grass and looks to the wind only to see nature; the second asks how one escapes birth and death when the light of the eyes falls to the ground; the third asks where one goes when the four elements separate. The text calls them 'three checkpoint sayings' (三關語) set up in the chamber to test students. A later public exchange invokes 'Doushuai's three-checkpoint sayings' and receives the invitation 'ask them one by one.' Their enumerated referents differ from Huanglong's buddha-hand, donkey-foot, and birth-circumstance questions.
Senses.Note: The phrase 'Doushuai's three checkpoints' (兜率三關) occurs in multiple allowlisted texts, while the full enumeration is anchored in Doushuai's governing section. The master key records a genuinely distinct named taxonomy.

Occurrences.Kwic: 室中設三關語以驗學者，其一曰：撥草瞻風，只圖見性。即今上人性在甚麼處？其二曰：識得自性，方脫生死。眼光落地時作麼生脫？其三曰：脫得生死，便知去處。四大分離向甚麼處去？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Doushuai's governing section enumerates all three of his checkpoint sayings.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「悟道雪山成話柄，惟明生死絕淆訛，曾聞兜率三關語，還許即今請益麼？」師云：「一一問將來。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later question invokes 'Doushuai's three-checkpoint sayings' and asks permission to inquire; the master answers, 'ask them one by one.'

AlternateTargets: what does that have to do with it?
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "what connection does that have?" The question occurs 114 times in 41 allowlisted texts. In public interviews it rejects a proposed connection between a master's words and the matter asked about: after a monk identifies the present master with an earlier house, the answer is "what connection does that have?" (有什麼交涉). The phrase also appears in prose criticism. The Blue Cliff Record says that treating Mazu's left and right eyes as the sun-face and moon-face has "what connection?" and that such readers have missed the old matter. Elsewhere a master asks, "if lips, voice, and appearances are taken as oneself, what connection does that have?" (若以唇吻聲色以為自己，有什麼交涉). In another exchange, a monk himself uses the question after the answer "the graph 'by means of'" (以字), and receives "the graph 'eight'" (八字), a spoken play on similar-sounding graph names. Zen bends an ordinary request for relevance into a compact interview verdict: the reply or explanation offered has not connected with the exchange.
Senses.Note: One interrogative/verdict sense covers the evidence. Different objects rejected by the question are not different meanings. The shorter variant "what connection?" (有甚交涉) belongs to the same family but is not included in the exact-headword count.

Occurrences.Kwic: 左眼是日面。右眼是月面。有什麼交涉。驢年未夢見在。只管蹉過古人事。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The comment rejects an eye-based explanation of Mazu's sun-face and moon-face saying and says it misses the old matter.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若以唇吻聲色以為自己，有什麼交涉？設使百千問難，秖益自勞；
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall statement asks what connection taking lips, voice, and appearances as oneself could have, then says hundreds of questions only add labor.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：恁麼則昔日智門，今朝和尚。師云：有什麼交涉？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk identifies the present master with Zhimen; the master replies, “what connection does that have?”

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：經文最初兩字是什麼字？師云：以字。僧曰：有什麼交涉？師云：八字。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The phrase is spoken by the monk inside a graph-name exchange: “by-means-of graph” and “eight graph.”

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the eyebrows (眉毛) fall out (墮落). The exact phrase occurs four times in four allowlisted texts; all four are preserved here. The wider family includes "the eyebrows fall" (眉毛落, 40 occurrences), "are the eyebrows still there?" (眉毛在麼, 79), and "the eyebrows become tangled together" (眉毛廝結, 129). Chan records use the loss of eyebrows as a stated consequence or accusation attached to handling Buddhist or Chan speech: one comment says that making a Buddhist teaching-discussion of a line "implicates Shimen, whose eyebrows fall out" (若作佛法商量，累他石門眉毛墮落); another points to "the place where Cuiyan's eyebrows fall out" while reviewing the Cuiyan exchange. A question joins the phrase to Danxia's burning of the wooden Buddha and asks why the monastery director's eyebrows fall out. The exact phrase is late and sparse, but its eyebrow-loss family is widely transmitted; the texts do not provide an anatomical explanation, and this entry adds none.
Senses.Note: All four exact witnesses are late records. The broader eyebrow formulas supply family breadth but are not substituted as occurrences for the exact headword. PreferredTarget remains literal; 'penalty for false teaching' is too narrow because the exact witnesses attach it to several different recorded speech/case contexts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 趨炎附暖底不顧爛額焦頭、添薪熾炭底那管眉毛墮落？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A rhetorical question asks who, while adding fuel to the blaze, cares whether the eyebrows fall out.

Occurrences.Kwic: 拈云：「若作佛法商量，累他石門眉毛墮落。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The commentator says that treating Shimen's line as Buddhist teaching-discussion implicates Shimen in eyebrow loss.

Occurrences.Kwic: 看這翠巖眉毛墮落處自救不了，復有三元龍象互相蹴踏，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later review points to where Cuiyan's eyebrows fall out in the transmitted exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「丹霞燒木佛，院主為甚麼眉毛墮落？」師云：「脫體風光。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public question connects Danxia's burning of the wooden Buddha with the monastery director's eyebrow loss; the answer is preserved without interpreting it.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "brows intertwined with one another." The phrase occurs 129 times in 80 allowlisted texts. The records use the bodily image for persons brought into exceptionally close conjunction: one master says that for five or six years he has had his brows intertwined with the assembly, yet in fact they have had "no traffic in rice or water" (五六年來雖則與諸人眉毛廝結，其實水米無交). Another requires "brows intertwined, sharing life and sharing death" (眉毛廝結，同生同死). It also appears as an answer in a public interview: asked for the phrase for opening the retreat, the master replies, "brows intertwined" (眉毛廝結). Elsewhere a hall address sets saying and silence against each other: "if one speaks, heaven and earth are far apart; if one does not speak, brows are intertwined" (說即天地懸殊，不說即眉毛廝結). The Chan use turns a physical impossibility into a compact, repeatable encounter phrase; the accompanying clauses establish proximity or conjunction but do not authorize this entry to decide what speakers intend by it.
Senses.Note: One idiomatic referent covers the sampled uses. Pairings with “no dealings,” “sharing life and death,” speech/silence, and retreat opening are distinct contexts, not distinct objects or word classes. No second sense is created from competing readings of the image.

Occurrences.Kwic: 五六年來雖則與諸人眉毛廝結，其實水米無交
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker says his brows have been intertwined with the assembly for years, yet they have had no traffic in rice or water.

Occurrences.Kwic: 直須眉毛廝結，同生同死。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The phrase is directly paired with “sharing life and sharing death.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「摩竭掩室、毘耶杜口則不問，即今天童結制一句，請師舉唱。」師云：「眉毛廝結。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked to proclaim a phrase for Tiantong's opening of the retreat, the master answers, “brows intertwined.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 說即天地懸殊，不說即眉毛廝結。說與不說，拈放一邊。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address contrasts speaking, when heaven and earth are far apart, with not speaking, when brows are intertwined, then sets both aside.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to raise something and ask. Chan records use it when a speaker carries a saying, exchange, or disputed comparison into a further interview and asks another master about it. Zhenjue raises before Xuanwu a description of light from the eye illuminating mountains and rivers, then asks where that person is at fault. Dongshan raises before Yunju the statement that there is no Maitreya in heaven or on earth; Yunju replies by asking who then gave him his name. Jiashan and Dingshan take their opposed sayings about buddha in birth-and-death to a master, and Jiashan raises the matter by asking whose view is more intimate; the answer distinguishes one as intimate and one as remote. Another monk raises the staff of Deshan and shout of Linji and asks what side they clarify; the master tells him to try to say, and tests his ensuing shout. The deviation is institutional and textual: raising is not merely lifting an object, but re-presenting prior words or actions to a Chan interlocutor so that the case continues through another public question and response.
Senses.Note: This compound includes both operations: “raise” (舉) re-presents prior material and “ask” (問) directs a question about it. It overlaps with “raise a case” (舉) and “question-and-answer” (問答), while differing from a master's newly bestowed question (垂問).

Occurrences.Kwic: 真覺大師舉問玄晤大師：「眼門放光，照破山河。山河大地，不礙眼光。此人過在什摩處，只欠濤汰。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhenjue raises a statement before Xuanwu and asks where the described person is at fault.

Occurrences.Kwic: 洞山舉問雲居，居云：天上無彌勒，地下無彌勒，未審誰與安名？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dongshan raises an earlier Maitreya statement before Yunju, whose response is another question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 二人上山參禮。夾山便舉問師。未審二人見處那箇較親。師云。一親一疎。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After two opposed sayings, Jiashan raises their views and asks which is more intimate; the master gives a paired verdict.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉問德山棒臨濟喝未審明得什麼邊事師云你試道看僧便喝師云瞎
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk raises Deshan's staff and Linji's shout for questioning; the master asks him to try to say and judges his shouted response.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to raise up and make prominent. The expression occurs 1,627 times in 275 allowlisted texts. Chan records make it a public teaching-seat verb: a master proclaims the sect's purport, presents 'this matter' before the assembly, or is asked in an interview to present a cited event. One opening discourse pairs opening the hall with 'proclaiming the teaching of the school'; another records a whisk transmitted with the charge to present this matter before the human and heavenly assembly. A later discourse says that one sentence had already been presented before the listeners entered the gate.
Senses.Note: No definition formula was found. The deviation is institutional and observable: the ordinary verb becomes a recurrent description of a master's public work from the teaching seat. The corpus does not support separate senses for different subjects raised; all are objects of the same transitive act.

Occurrences.Kwic: 爍破重關，徹法源底，逼得山僧無藏隱處，今日不免對眾舉揚。煩維那宣讀。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master says he cannot avoid presenting it publicly before the assembly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 為國開堂，舉揚宗教，山僧不敢囊藏被葢
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An opening-hall discourse pairs the ceremony with proclaiming the teaching of the school.

Occurrences.Kwic: 擲鉢峰前事，請師為舉揚。師云：風不來，樹不動。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk publicly asks the master to present an earlier event, and the master answers.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸人未入門時，一句子已向汝舉揚了也，更待興問酬荅
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse says one sentence had already been presented before question and response began.

Occurrences.Kwic: 付與山僧，曰：『向後人天眾前舉揚個事去。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A transmitted whisk accompanies an explicit charge to present this matter before the assembly.
